name: An interview with Sonam Pakistan's new Dean

content.text: Dr David Arthur, the new dean of the Aga Khan University's School of Nursing and Midwifery in Pakistan has three decades of research and practice in nursing.

A specialist in mental health nursing, Dr Arthur's clinical and academic career has spanned hospitals and rural communities in Australia, Hong Kong, the Philippines, Singapore and now, Pakistan. During this time, he has witnessed major changes in the role of nurses in providing healthcare and led efforts to promote family and community-focused approaches to treatment.
While he describes mental health as his passion; his interests also include community service, architecture and sports such as cricket and tennis.
In this interview, Dr Arthur outlines his vision for Sonam, tells us about the progress he's noticed in the profession and shares what has made his time at AKU special.
Tell us what inspired you to begin a career in nursing.

I was 17 years old, when a high school friend went through serious mental health challenges with depression and unpredictable behavior. His behavior and moods were very different from what we were all used to and he was rejected by most of his friends. His family had trouble managing him too and he became involved in antisocial behavior and eventually committed suicide.

His family was devastated. The experience of seeing his loved ones cope with his ups and downs remained with me and I became deeply interested in finding out how to ensure that all people get the support and if necessary, treatment, that's appropriate to them. That was one of the reasons that made me chose nursing as my field of study.
Tell us about the changes you've noticed in nursing over the years.

There have been major changes in where nurses treat patients, particularly in my specialty of mental health nursing. When I started my career in Australia in the 1980s, those suffering from mental disorders were viewed very negatively. They were isolated from the rest of society and treated in closed-off wards in punitive settings. You'd get a sense that nurses were monitoring dangerous people rather than caring for the ill.

Over time, as mental health issues became more common, you saw a rise in the number of outpatient clinics that are now common in most hospitals. Patients would now visit healthcare centres alongside their families. This meant that nurses now played a more active role in making patients and their families comfortable through skillful communication and by teaching relatives how to support their loved one.

An increasing emphasis on nurses being advocates for patients and the advent of community-based approaches meant that treatment moved beyond the traditional hospital setting and into communities. This is where nurses can make a significant difference as witnessing a community's healthcare challenges enables them to implement preventive healthcare measures which lead to great benefits for society.

Today's nurses specialise in a variety of fields such as oncology, critical care and geriatrics. They are much more alert to warnings signs in different kinds of patients. This specialist information means they are better able to support families in creating an environment that enables recovery.
So there have been 'setting' and treatment changes?

Yes. There has been great progress in treatment methods which have moved from a focus on invasive methods such as electro-convulsive therapy and surgery towards counseling, alternative therapies and family-based approaches to nursing.

There are now a much wider range of therapies available. Psychosocial approaches - where treatment takes into account the patient's surroundings - means that mental health is rightly being viewed as a product of one's surroundings. By involving the family in treatment we've seen a huge improvement in how post-natal conditions, adolescent anxiety and schizophrenia are treated.

The application of motivational techniques and cognitive behavioural therapy - challenging negative thought patterns to help alter behaviour - have empowered patients to take control of their lives rather than rely on medicine.

There is also a growing realisation that patients benefit from having a relaxed state of mind and by being focused in their thinking. This has made therapeutic approaches such as mindfulness, where patients are taught to focus on the present instead of being preoccupied with the past or future, more accepted and popular.
How are we different from developed countries?

Community-based services in the developing world are lagging behind more prosperous countries. This limits the access of rural populations to healthcare and so nurses based in remote settings need to be taught distinct skills to tackle issues facing underprivileged communities. This should be a priority for the developing world. I've also noticed that the effects of substance abuse - both drugs and alcohol - are problems that health systems need to be geared to tackle.
So, what is the role the School should play?

The Aga Khan University has a reputation for excellence in nursing and a track-record of setting standards in the field. I look forward to us becoming stronger leaders in education, research and practice in Pakistan and our region, and with our School in East Africa enhancing our international reputation. I hope to inspire the institution to develop a wider range of specialty programmes so that our graduates can provide innovative nursing practice to tackle today's healthcare challenges. A specialised degree for mental health nursing at the master's level is something I believe would be of great value.
That's work, what about your other interests?

Eight years ago my wife Lynn and I started an initiative in an underprivileged area in southern Philippines. Poverty in the area has resulted in a range of persistent healthcare problems tied to lack of education, poor diet, unhealthy lifestyle and reduced access to health care. A severe shortage of trained healthcare professionals in the area means that there is a great need for solutions to these challenges.

So I started a programme in which interdisciplinary healthcare students from Australia and other countries visit the area and experience its challenges first-hand. They are then trained to design healthcare interventions to help tackle the root causes of disease and to improve healthcare practices in the area. So far we've had 250 students complete the programme and it's been a very satisfying experience.
Any more interests you'd like to share?

I've always been a cricket fan and I was inspired by the great performances of cricketers like Denis Lillee, Allan Border and Imran Khan. Growing up in Australia, I had the honour of being coached by cricket greats like Ian and Greg Chappell too. When I moved to Hong Kong, the local enthusiasm for cricket brought out my love for the game and saw me get involved in organising international tournaments and developing the local cricket scene.

I used be to the secretary of the Kowloon Cricket Club and I helped put together the Hong Kong Sixes - an annual tournament in which teams from ten countries around the world such as Pakistan, India and Australia - competed. One of my most memorable experiences was seeing cricket legend Richard Hadlee coach the Hong Kong cricket team.
